name: Glass Green
lede: Glass Green is a pale, slightly yellow green first set down by Ridgway in 1912 and repeated independently in both the ISCC-NBS and Maerz and Paul dictionaries.

sections.title: Three dictionaries, one green
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* places Glass Green on plate XXXI, hue 29 double-prime, tone d [1]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary carries an independent record of the same name back to 1790, on plate 18, swatch F3 [1]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files it as a light yellow green, block 119 [1]. Why the color was called 'glass' is undocumented in the sources we checked [1].

The nearest named colors on file are [[amber-white]], [[primrose-yellow]] and [[baryta-yellow]], at 2.8, 3.8 and 3.8 ΔE [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
A color within six units of Glass Green covers at least five percent of the canvas in 528 of our 23,781 paintings, 2.22 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens narrows that to 319 [2]. That ranks it ahead of 77 percent of the named colors we track [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 33 of 1,674 paintings, at 2.0 percent of that decade's paintings, 1.8 times the archive's overall rate, and it most often plays a light, in 67 percent of its 319 appearances [2].

Arnoud van Halen is its most devoted painter, using it in nine of his 50 paintings here, 4.9 times the rate of the museums those works come from [2]. It shares canvases with [[courge-green|Courge Green]] and [[dull-citrine|Dull Citrine]] more than chance would predict, with lifts of 8.7 and 5.7 [2]. The earliest matching painting dates to 1413, almost exactly 499 years before Ridgway recorded the name in 1912 — a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof the color existed as a pigment that early, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2].

origin.first_recorded: 1790, per Maerz and Paul (1930); standardized by Ridgway, 1912
